data.text:
# Slice 2: the comparison is scoped, and the measurement says SEEN-112 stays blocked

RED is record 12 and GREEN is record 13, 246 tests with 6 failures and 5 errors, then 246 OK; the full suite
is 1,176. The RED's three voices: "The tree moved under check 3: it ran against fc1b2cc72c1c and this record
is written against 8c988de3b054", which is the whole-tree comparison as the stated reason and the state every
real journal is in; "'harness/slice_one.py' not found in ..."; and "'whole tree' not found in ..." with
`module 'harness.gates' has no attribute 'content_fingerprint'`.

The scoped refusal now reads: "The code check {n} covers has changed since it ran: harness/slice_one.py. Its
slice names harness/slice_one.py, and its evidence is about those files as they were, not as they are; run it
again in this attempt". The fallback names why it fell back, either that the citation names no slice or that
no commit on the branch carries the tree the check ran against. The regression is deliberately left on the
whole-tree rule, because it covers the suite rather than a slice.

A slice entry naming a directory carries everything under it, kept on purpose: git's own pathspec does the
matching, so `supabase/migrations` reaches every migration and not `supabase/migrations-old`, and the
direction here is the opposite of the guard's, where a wider scope grants permission. A wider scope can only
cost a citation its evidence, never grant it. Two tests pin both halves.

**The measured answer on SEEN-112, which is the reason this ticket existed: no, and scoping is not what stops
it.** Running the implemented logic over its branch: slice 1's green 11 ran against `cdadefa` and is refused
because `harness/cli.py`, `harness/loop.py`, `harness/paths.py` and `harness/tests/test_loop.py` moved; slice
2's green 15 ran against `4a1ba10` and is refused because three of those four moved; both slices' REDs ran
against trees no commit carries, so they fall back to the whole tree and are refused there. The same verdicts
hold against attempt 5's advance point and against the branch tip. **The refusals are correct.** Attempts 3
and 4 reworked exactly the files those slices named, so that evidence really is about code the ticket has
changed since. The rule did what it was built to do and the answer it gives is no.

**One structural finding, named and not worked around.** A cross-attempt RED can never pass a content test,
by construction: a red runs against the pre-fix tree, and the very files its slice names must change before
its green, or the green would not be green. On SEEN-112, none of the five red trees is carried by any commit,
against three of five green trees. Since a tdd record needs a red and a green per slice, it can never accept
a real cross-attempt slice pair. Slice 1's whole-tree rule has the same defect; scoping only made it visible.
The next step is to judge a slice's pair by its green, because a red's standing is already carried by the
ordering rule and by its own recorded failure, or to record per-file blobs on each check. Neither is this
ticket: a third amendment to reach a case the measurement says is out of reach anyway would be the motivated
reasoning this ticket was warned about. It goes in the Outcome as the named next step.

One duplication to own: `content_fingerprint` reads the fingerprint definition a second time, because
`harness/repository.py` is outside the slice's files. It is pinned by a test that requires the two readings
to agree, and its honest home is `Repository`.
